name: SULLIVAN, JUSTICE
description: Concurred, argued that Hyatt III does not apply to municipal entities like JEA, and neither the Full Faith and Credit Clause nor comity mandates dismissal, allowing Promenade's case to proceed.

name: COLEMAN, JUSTICE
description: Concurred, argued that Section 273(3) of the Mississippi Constitution is unworkable with fewer than five congressional districts, rendering the Initiative 65 petition insufficient and its certification void.

name: MAXWELL, JUSTICE
description: Dissented, argued that the majority's interpretation judicially kills Mississippi's citizen initiative process by injecting a federal court's injunction into the state constitution, and that under Mississippi law, there are still five congressional districts for state purposes.

name: CHAMBERLIN, JUSTICE
description: Dissented, argued that the constitution is presumed capable of ordering human affairs and that Section 273(3) is workable if interpreted to use the five congressional districts as they existed in 1992, which would preserve the people's right to amend the constitution by initiative.

name: KITCHENS, P.J.
description: Dissented, argued that the constitution is presumed capable of ordering human affairs and that Section 273(3) is workable if interpreted to use the five congressional districts as they existed in 1992, which would preserve the people's right to amend the constitution by initiative.

name: GRIFFIS, JUSTICE
description: Concurred, argued that the NCAA neither denied Farrar's due-process rights nor maliciously interfered with his prospective business relations, and therefore summary judgment for NCAA was appropriate.

name: RANDOLPH, C.J.
description: Dissented, argued that there were too many unresolved factual questions regarding the NCAA's procedures and potential malicious interference to grant summary judgment.

name: KING, P.J.
description: Dissented, argued that the Court prioritizes efficiency over justice, violates the oath to administer justice without respect to persons, and infringes upon indigent defendants' fundamental right to access the courts by imposing monetary sanctions and filing restrictions.

name: KITCHENS, P.J.
description: Dissented, argued that rather than restricting Walter's access to the courts, the petition should simply be found to lack merit.

name: CHAMBERLIN
description: Concurred, argued that PPS lacked standing because they failed to demonstrate an adverse impact different from the general public, and the federal ARPA funds were not earmarked for educational purposes nor commingled with state funds.

name: BEAM, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the court is not ruling on state funds but American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funds, which were not earmarked by either the federal or state government for any educational purposes, so PPS cannot claim harm.

name: KING, P.J.
description: Dissented, argued that PPS has standing due to an adverse effect its members experience from the competitive advantage given to private schools and due to taxpayer standing, and that Senate Bills 2780 and 3064 are unconstitutional.

name: KITCHENS, P.J.
description: Dissented, argued that PPS has standing and that Senate Bills 2780 and 3064 are unconstitutional, joining Presiding Justice King's opinion.

name: GRIFFIS, JUSTICE
description: Concurred, argued that JFT failed to establish standing, either in its own right or through associate standing, because it did not provide direct evidence of current JPS employees as members at the time of litigation.

name: COLEMAN, J.
description: Dissented, argued that JFT had standing because ample evidence showed it was a legitimate organization adversely impacted by JPS policies, and direct evidence of membership is not always required, especially when it is common knowledge.

name: KITCHENS, P.JJ.
description: Dissented, argued that JFT had standing, the issue was not moot, and multiple free speech violations occurred, thus the trial court's judgment should be affirmed.

name: KING, P.JJ.
description: Dissented, argued that JFT had standing, the issue was not moot, and multiple free speech violations occurred, thus the trial court's judgment should be affirmed.

name: MAXWELL, JUSTICE
description: Concurred, arguing that House Bill 1020, Section 1, violated the constitutional requirement for elected judges, while Section 4 and Section 9-1-105(2) are constitutional as they establish an inferior court with appellate oversight and allow for temporary judicial appointments for emergencies.

name: KITCHENS, P.J.
description: Concurred in part and dissented in part, arguing that the CCID court is unconstitutional due to the Legislature's failure to provide a statutory mechanism for supervision by a constitutional court.

name: KING, P.J.
description: Concurred in part and dissented in part, joining Presiding Justice Kitchens' opinion regarding the unconstitutionality of the CCID court.

name: David M. Ishee
description: Concurred with the majority opinion, finding Brown's petition successive, barred by res judicata, frivolous, and warranting sanctions.

name: KING, PRESIDING JUSTICE
description: Dissented, argued that the Court prioritizes efficiency over justice, infringes on constitutional rights by restricting indigent defendants' access to the court system, and punishes them for filing petitions.

name: KITCHENS, P.J.
description: Dissented, argued that the Court should have simply found the petition lacked merit instead of restricting Brown's access to the courts.

name: Dawn H. Beam
description: Concurred, argued that Brunson's petition was time-barred, successive, without merit, and frivolous, justifying denial and restriction of future in forma pauperis filings.

name: KITCHENS, P.J.
description: Dissented, argued that while the petition lacked merit, restricting an indigent defendant's access to courts violates constitutional rights and prioritizes efficiency over justice.

name: KING, P.J.
description: Dissented, argued that while the petition lacked merit, restricting an indigent defendant's access to courts violates constitutional rights and prioritizes efficiency over justice.

name: KING, P.J.
description: Dissented, argued that restricting indigent defendants from filing future petitions in forma pauperis prioritizes efficiency over justice, violates constitutional rights, and punishes the poor.

name: KITCHENS, P.J.
description: Dissented, argued that restricting indigent defendants from filing future petitions in forma pauperis prioritizes efficiency over justice, violates constitutional rights, and punishes the poor.

name: KING, P.J.
description: Dissented, argued that imposing monetary sanctions and restricting access for indigent defendants punishes them and violates constitutional rights, prioritizing efficiency over justice, and that the court's decision violates Johnson's state constitutional right to access courts.

name: KITCHENS, P.J.
description: Dissented, joined KING, P.J.'s separate written statement.

name: KING, PRESIDING JUSTICE
description: Concurred, argued that general consent to search a person extends to closed containers found on that person, and Buford was not illegally detained.

name: COLEMAN, JUSTICE
description: Concurred, argued that the reduction to four congressional districts made the signature distribution requirement of Section 273(3) unworkable, invalidating Initiative 65.

name: MAXWELL, JUSTICE
description: Dissented, argued that the majority's interpretation judicially kills the citizen-initiative process by wrongly applying a federal injunction to state constitutional law, which still recognizes five congressional districts.

name: CHAMBERLIN, JUSTICE
description: Dissented, argued that the majority's ruling destroys the presumption that the Constitution can order human affairs and that Section 273(3) should be interpreted based on the five congressional districts existing in 1992 to preserve the initiative process.

name: KITCHENS, P.J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority's ruling destroys the presumption that the Constitution can order human affairs and that Section 273(3) should be interpreted based on the five congressional districts existing in 1992 to preserve the initiative process.
